title: Does Prayer Change Anything?
excerpt: Scripture commands asking, records that some things happened because people asked, and keeps the prayers that were refused, including one prayed in a garden by Jesus himself.
body:
A mother spent four months in a hospital waiting room asking God for one thing, and she drove home without her son. A man prayed for work and was hired the same week, and he has never known what to say to the friend who prayed the same prayer and lost his house. A girl of nine was told that God always answers, and she is keeping a private count. And a skeptic who has watched all of this says what the other three are afraid to say: when the prayer is granted you call it an answer, when it is refused you call it a mystery, and a belief that is confirmed by every possible result has not been tested by any of them.

The skeptic's charge is the strongest one, and it deserves a real answer. The mother's question is the heaviest, and no answer here will be offered to her as an explanation.

One thing comes before any of it. The site's page for those facing a terminal diagnosis, speaking of the ways Christians read the promise in James about prayer for the sick, says this: "None of these readings sets prayer against medical care, and none makes an unhealed believer guilty of too little faith. Paul prayed three times and was not healed, and no one in Scripture blames him." And the site's note on that passage adds: "Anyone who is sick, in pain, or in despair should call on both the church and qualified medical help, and anyone thinking of harming themselves should reach out immediately to a trusted person or to emergency services." [Find Help](/help) lists places to turn.

## The Case Against

It starts with what Jesus said, because the promises are not modest. "Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you" (Matthew 7:7). "Whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours" (Mark 11:24). "If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it" (John 14:14). A reader who takes those sentences at face value and then looks at a children's cancer ward has every right to ask what happened.

Then come the church's replies, which the skeptic knows by heart. God answers every prayer: yes, no, or wait. You must not have had enough faith. It wasn't his will. Each reply can be true in a given case. Taken together they form a net with no holes, in which anything that happens counts as support. People remember the prayer that was followed by a recovery and forget the ones that were followed by a funeral.

Under the experience lies an older problem of logic. Thomas Aquinas stated it in the thirteenth century, against himself, more cleanly than most skeptics do. Prayer seems meant to tell God what we need, and he already knows. Prayer seems meant to move him, and "God's mind is unchangeable and inflexible." So either God was going to do the good thing anyway, and the asking added nothing, or the asking changed his mind, and he was about to do something less than good.

## What Has to Be Granted

A great deal of that has to be granted. The three replies have been used as excuses, and the one about faith has been said at bedsides where it did real harm. Many prayers for plainly good things have been refused. Nobody can show, in a way that would satisfy a neutral observer, that a particular recovery was an answer and would not have come without the prayer. The believer and the skeptic are looking at the same event.

The Bible has to be credited with something the skeptic may not expect. It records the failures itself. King David fasted and lay all night on the ground for his sick child, and the child died (2 Samuel 12:16–23). Paul wrote of a thorn in his flesh, "Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me" (2 Corinthians 12:8), and it did not leave. The prophet Habakkuk opens his book with a complaint: "O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear?" (Habakkuk 1:2). Psalm 88 is a prayer from start to finish, and unlike nearly every other lament in the book it never turns to praise. Its last line is "my companions have become darkness" (Psalm 88:18). The people who wrote these books knew that prayers go unanswered.

## What the Promises Were

The sweeping sentences have a setting, and it changes how they read without making them small. Jesus speaks of asking "in my name." His disciple John writes that "if we ask anything according to his will he hears us" (1 John 5:14). James tells people who are fighting over what they want, "You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions" (James 4:3).

The skeptic will say that this is the fine print arriving late, and that a promise hedged with "according to his will" can never fail. He is right that it can't be run as an experiment. But nobody in the New Testament offers prayer as an experiment. When Jesus gives the promise in Matthew 7, his picture is a child asking a father for bread. A father is a person. He can be asked, he can be moved, and he can say no for reasons the child can't see, which a vending machine cannot. The promise is that the Father hears and that he gives good things. It was never that the one who asks holds the controls.

That doesn't remove the mother's question, because what she asked for was good.

## Whether It Changes Anything

Scripture says that it does, and says so in stories that make careful theologians uneasy. After the golden calf, God tells Moses he will destroy Israel. Moses pleads. "And the LORD relented from the disaster that he had spoken of bringing on his people" (Exodus 32:14). King Hezekiah is told by a prophet that he will die of his illness; he turns his face to the wall and prays, and the prophet is sent back: "I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will heal you" (2 Kings 20:5). James, who has just warned against asking wrongly, also says, "You do not have, because you do not ask" (James 4:2). The plain meaning is that some things are not given because nobody asked for them.

And the same Jesus who commands asking says, a few lines before the Lord's Prayer, "your Father knows what you need before you ask him" (Matthew 6:8). He gives that as a reason to pray simply and never as a reason to stop. Scripture leaves both sentences standing, and the traditions have had to hold them together.

## How the Traditions Hold It Together

The oldest answer is the one Aquinas gave to his own objection. God's providence, he wrote, settles what will happen and also by what causes it will happen, and human acts are among the causes. The comparison with a farmer is close at hand. A man who plants is not trying to overrule God's plan for the harvest; planting is how the harvest was planned to come. Prayer works the same way. "For we pray not that we may change the Divine disposition, but that we may impetrate that which God has disposed to be fulfilled by our prayers." To impetrate is to obtain by asking. On this account there are things God has decided to give through prayer and in no other way, so a prayer truly obtains something, and no change takes place in God.

The Reformed tradition, which puts the greatest weight on God's sovereignty, says the same and then goes further. The Westminster Confession holds that "God, in his ordinary providence, maketh use of means." John Calvin answered the charge that prayer is pointless by saying that God "has appointed it not so much for his own sake as for ours": the asking teaches the one who asks where every good thing comes from. And the Heidelberg Catechism of 1563 states flatly that God gives his grace and Spirit "only to those who constantly and with heartfelt longing ask Him for these gifts." A tradition often accused of making prayer useless teaches that some gifts are given only to those who ask.

Other Christians think those accounts still leave too little room for the stories. Many in the Wesleyan and Arminian traditions stress that God has made some outcomes truly depend on human asking. Some go further and hold that the future is partly open even to God, so that, in the words of the site's study of the question, "the texts where he relents mean exactly what they say." Still others hold that God knew from eternity what every person would freely pray in every circumstance and ordered the world with those prayers in view.

Each account has a question it finds hard. The classical one is asked whether anything was ever really open: if the prayer and its answer were both fixed from eternity, in what sense did Moses change anything? The open one is asked how a God who waits to see what will be asked can promise how the story ends. This is a second-order question, on which faithful churches differ. The site's note on Hezekiah, weighing two readings of his story, gives the common ground in one sentence: "Both views agree that prayer is not a formality and that God's purposes include the prayers of his people."

## The Prayer That Was Refused

None of that touches the waiting room, and the Bible seems to know it. Its fullest treatment of unanswered prayer is a scene in a garden, where the one praying is Jesus.

On the night of his arrest he asked to be spared. "Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will" (Mark 14:36). Mark says that "he fell on the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him" (Mark 14:35). No lack of faith can be found in that prayer, and nothing wrong in the asking. He asked for a good thing, his life. The cup was not removed. By the next afternoon he was praying the first line of a psalm: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46).

The letter to the Hebrews makes a claim about that night which is easy to pass over. Jesus "offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence" (Hebrews 5:7). He was heard, and he died anyway. The answer he was given was the resurrection, which came after the thing he had begged to be spared and did not replace it.

That gives the mother no reason, and anyone who uses it as one has misused it. It establishes something narrower. In the Christian account, a refused prayer is no proof that the one praying was unloved, unheard or short of faith, because all three would then have to be said of Christ. And it means that the God to whom she is speaking knows what it is to ask and be refused.

Paul's own refusal came with words. "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). The site's note on that chapter is careful about how far this goes. It is no rule that God never heals. "It is an honest testimony that God sometimes answers prayer for relief with grace to endure, and that such an answer is not a sign of his absence." Some who have prayed for healing will say that this is what they were given. Others will say they were given nothing they could name, and the psalms have room for them too. For the person who has run out of words altogether, Paul wrote that "we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words" (Romans 8:26).

Three men in the book of Daniel, facing a furnace, said the rest of it. "Our God whom we serve is able to deliver us," they told the king. "But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods" (Daniel 3:17–18). In those two sentences they claim no certainty about the outcome and they refuse to make their faith depend on it.

## What We Have Done to the Sick

The church's guilt here is plain. We have told the sick that they would be well if they believed harder, and we have told the bereaved that God needed another angel or that everything happens for a reason. The first is the cruelty of Job's friends, who were sure his suffering proved something about him. At the end of that book God says to them, "you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7). Job had spent most of the book complaining.

A whole school of preaching has been built on the first error. It teaches that health and money are promised to faith and that those who lack them have failed to claim them. It is not a harmless exaggeration. It turns every hospital bed into an accusation, and Paul's thorn, Timothy's bad stomach and the cross itself stand against it.

We have also set prayer against medicine, as though calling a doctor were a failure of trust. Scripture never does. James sends the sick to the elders for prayer and for oil, which in his day was itself a medicine. Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach, and one of his closest companions was a physician. The site's note on James says of its promise: "What the passage does not teach is that illness that persists is a sign of weak faith or hidden sin."

One more evasion needs naming, because thoughtful Christians reach for it. It is the saying that prayer doesn't change things, it changes us. Half of that is true. Paul promises that those who bring their requests to God will be given a peace "which surpasses all understanding" (Philippians 4:7), and he does not promise the thing requested. But as a full answer it gives the skeptic everything he asked for while sounding devout. Jesus did not tell his disciples to ask so that they would feel better. He told them to ask for bread.

## What Can Be Said

Christians confess together that God hears, that he has commanded his people to ask and to keep asking, that he is a Father and is free to refuse, and that no one who suffers is to be told the fault is in their faith. How his eternal purpose and a real request fit together is argued among them, and the argument will go on.

Does prayer change anything? Scripture says that some things happen because people asked. It does not say which ones, and it gives no method for telling afterward. That will not satisfy the skeptic, and it should not be dressed up to look as if it could. What Christians have is a command, a promise about the character of the one they are asking, and a record of people who asked and were refused and kept speaking to him.

Jesus told a story about a widow who kept coming to a judge, "to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart" (Luke 18:1). He ended it with a question that he left unanswered. "When the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?" (Luke 18:8).

Psalm 88 is in the Bible. Someone prayed it in the dark and got nothing back, and God's people were given it to pray again, word for word, as Scripture. The mother's prayer has a place in that book. Nothing in it tells her why.

*"O LORD, why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face from me?"* (Psalm 88:14)

*"Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will."* (Mark 14:36)
